utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. There are protective measures for this witness which has the effect that members -- in this courtroom, that members of the public are not able to be present because of the physical configuration of this courtroom. The Chamber would mention that a Mr. van Odijk will by order of the Chamber be able to view the proceedings. He is a representative from Utrecht which the Chamber is meeting today, and in those circumstances, he will be, by special order, able to view the proceedings in our physical arrangements from what would normally be the public gallery. If the witness could be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I remind you the affirmation that you made to speak the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Kravetz. Oh, we are well past you, Ms. Kravetz. Mr. Djurdjic. I had completely lost you in the cloud of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel, sir. Before I go on with putting my questions to the Colonel, I should like to inform the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution has agreed to redacted proposal regarding exhibits used in the Milutinovic case except for one which was taken off the list which I will be using in the cross-examination. Ms. Kravetz was very fair in that regard, so that we can continue or should Ms. Kravetz agree to that as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We are happy to take your assurance in her presence that she is in agreement. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I should like to ask you in connection with the telegrams that we referred to yesterday, the initials DA refer to whom?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The DA is defence attache, which is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I should like to ask you a question in connection with a part of your statement yesterday in which you stated that you made some photographs in Donje Prekaze in March 1998. Did you see those photographs during the proceedings here before this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember to be honest whether they came before the Court or not. As you know, I've made several appearances here, but I cannot verify that they came before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But they have not been shown to you on this particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I am aware, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document D005-0657 brought up on the screen. Paragraph 20 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is the statement which you gave to the investigators from the 5th to the 7th of December, 2000. I would kindly ask you to take a look a paragraph 20, in which it is stated -- was that: "It's likely that there were paramilitaries such as Arkan's Tigers in Kosovo, I was never able to make a positive identification. Members of all units, the VJ, JSO, the PJP and the SAJ, involving in Kosovo wore bandanas around their heads and other types of non-standard kit to varying degrees. Under such circumstances, it would not have been surprising for members of these units to be mistaken as members of paramilitaries."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just want to point out that the protective measures that apply to this witness include the redaction of some personal details on the cover page of the statements that are used during his testimony, and I was just seeing that the version that is being used, at least in the the B/C/S, in the e-court system does not contain those redactions, and the redactions that had been granted by the Milosevic Chamber in 2002 were the redactions of his place of birth and date of birth. So if my learned colleague is going to be using any prior statements, those details should be redacted from the first page of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The issue will be whether a redaction is possible from the e-court version before it comes up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will deal with the matter by not broadcasting the exhibit publicly. Carry on please, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does the passage which I've just read out reflect what you stated to the investigators in December 2000, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. What I'm trying to convey is that in this particular situation there was a room for misidentification of various forces, and I was, therefore, using my own intelligence and observation to make this particular statement, if you will, in Defence of the Vojska Yugoslavia because there were journalists travelling throughout Kosovo, as you are well aware, who were making claims possibly based on their experience in former Balkan conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Colonel. Colonel, you say that you have direct knowledge of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, so I should like to ask you kindly to describe for me a village, a typical Albanian village house that you visited, if you visited such houses.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited many -- most of the villages within Kosovo itself, having spent nearly, from 1996 to 1999, nearly three years in Kosovo. A typical Albanian village could consist of as many as or as little as three to five houses, or the hamlets or villages could be as many as 100. Some of these houses were what one would call peasant cottages, others were extremely big buildings showing the prosperous nature of trade within Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. What I'm interested in is these typical houses in Kosova-Metohija are called towers, so bearing in mind what you have just said that there would be a couple of houses in a village, were there any walls encircling those houses, of what material were those walls and what were they like, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many of the houses had a walled enclosure in which the family would live, perhaps many families. And this was a -- very much a typical example of Albanian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was it customary bearing in mind the fact that the largest percentage of the Albanians were Muslim faith, that as a rule there were no windows facing the streets, or facing a vantage point from which one could see the interior of the house, in other words?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say some of the houses were like that, sir. Others had windows facing the street or facing any other direction. I mean, yes, they were very private houses and very prosperous houses, some of them, as I've already said. I think man ever since he started has built a house and surrounded himself for normal protection in order to keep his family safe, and this is the particular way that the Albanian people do it, and yeah, very nice for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you agree with me when I say that also in 1998 -- both in 1998 and -- 1998 and 1999 most of the conflict in Kosovo took place in the rural areas between the KLA and the forces of the FRY?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I can't agree with that. There were -- there was conflict. It began in the Drenica area to the west of Pristina about 25, 30 kilometres. It then spread as the conflict grew and the areas of -- in Pec and Djakovica were destroyed, the Albanian areas. So it came into the towns, into -- both into the town and the rural areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us that you saw devastated villages and you never referred to any damaged towns.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall I was asked to, sir, but as I've just stated, I went to Djakovica and the entire Albanian market area was destroyed. If I remember correctly, in about August, July/August 1998, and the same took place in Pec. Also I think in Mitrovica and in Urosevac, to my memory, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When resistance was being offered from the houses that is you described, what were they in your perception, in terms of military fortifications?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these were not military fortifications, sir. These were normal houses. If we go back to Donje Prekaze, the Jashari family house was a normal Albanian house with a walled garden around it which if as a soldier you were attacking, yes, it could resemble a fort. But in fact, it was a normal civilian house as we've been describing. So to a soldier, yes, it's an objective which he may have been ordered to take or destroy, but in real life, it is another house. Another person's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. We are talking about civilian houses, but if they are being used for military purposes, if defence and resistance are being offered from those houses, it is in that sense that I ask you whether the facilities were well fortified.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree. I mean, to widen the discussion in other conflict areas, Northern Ireland, for instance, we would be shot at from houses. If you are going to be shot at, if you are sensible, you tend to put bricks and mortar between you and the person who is going to shoot at you to give you protection. That doesn't mean to say that the house is a protected house. So inevitably, houses will get damaged, property will get damaged if, if a fire fight develops around this objective, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me how did the KLA offer resistance to the forces or the FRY when there was fighting, and did you ever eye-witness any combat action yourself?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA had fortifications all the way down the road from outside of Orahovac to one of their major headquarters at Malisevo. These were trenches dug alongside the road on vantage points as normal defensive positions. Did I observe fighting? As I've stated in my reports, many times. I was present when shell fire was being directed at various areas: Junik, Prilep, Riznik, many other villages around Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Junik and the shelling of it. How far were you from Junik when you observed that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think if I remember correctly, about 1 or 2 kilometres. I could see the town of Junik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've just now told us that you were about a kilometre or two away from it. What was the time that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I mean the month.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I've drafted over 80 reports, I've made several appearances in front of the court, I would not wish to mislead the Court. I am afraid you'll have to refer back to the reports that I made. I cannot recall individual reports some 12 years ago. Junik was probably, in a guess, sometime between May, June, July of 1998. But I don't wish to be specific because I -- much water has gone under the bridge since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now have Exhibit D7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That will be, sir, a piece of video footage showing the visit of Mr. Holbrooke to Junik in June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Top it right there, please, for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, is this the kind of wall which is typical of compounds enclosing houses in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say it's fairly typical, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you notice that this is footage of Albanian television about the visit of Mr. Holbrooke in June 1998. Am I right when I say that we never saw any devastation in this footage that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But I shall be fair, and I'm going to show you another video which is from - just bear with me for a second - 16th of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the use of this video. We have not received any information from the Defence as to the providence of this video. We don't know who filmed it, when it was filmed, where it was filmed. We have simply been informed of -- given a date and a locality, but we have no way of verifying that it's accurate. So I will object to the use of this video during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is this an exhibit already, Mr. Djurdjic? I think you said it was Exhibit D7.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, it is D7, and it has already been used. And now we are going to view Junik, the 16th of August, 1998. It was received from the RTS, radio television Serbia, the other videos, that is. But this one from the 16th of August, I believe, was used by the Defence -- no, all the remaining three are by RTS, and the 16th of June one. And they were obtained through the national council for cooperation with the International Tribunal of The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the one that you have just shown an exhibit in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. D7 is the first video that we saw. It has been tendered and admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm told, Ms. Kravetz, it was admitted on the 30th of January, this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not objecting to the use of D7 which is the video we just saw; it's to the use of the subsequent videos that my learned colleague intends to use which have been listed in his notification for cross-examination for this witness. And I'm objecting on the grounds that I have just stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, all the videos were on our cross-examination list. I have not brought any new exhibits now. They have been entered into e-court and submitted to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They haven't previously been tendered, these remaining videos; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, they have not. That is what I'm about to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will see whether the witness is able to sufficiently identify what is displayed for the Chamber to be able to accept them as an exhibit. For that purpose, you may show them to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you recognise Junik from these buildings and streets that were just shown?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an impossible question to answer. I mean, that is very typical of the area in Kosova-Metohija, as you well know. That could have been anywhere within Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's continue. Colonel, you said yesterday that in mid-1998, 50 per cent of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija was controlled by the KLA. Is that correct, did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir. I did qualify it by saying control in what was, throughout 1998 and 1999, a very moving, fluid situation. But they had blocked the three of the main roads across Kosovo, as I indicated yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit D002-4026.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, could you please mark that area of Kosovo and Metohija on the map which was controlled by the KLA before the start of the summer offensive.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map is barely readable to be quite honest. But if this is Pristina here then Mitrovica, I presume, is up in this area. The northern road was blocked roughly in the area of Rudnik, which is about here. The middle and main route from Pristina to Pec was blocked approximately at Lapusnik, roughly in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can I ask you to pause there, and if you could mark the areas that you have identified in progressive numerical order so we start with number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, 1 is at the top here, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the route from Mitrovica through a place called Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you mark with number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With great respect, Your Honour, this map is virtually -- well, is unreadable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To my eyesight, it is not readable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rudnik, sir, is roughly in this area here where I put 2. Roughly, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next route is from Pristina where I've put the 2, running through Pristina across the middle of Kosovo with Drenica to the north and coming towards Pec in the west over here, if that is Pec. I think Pec might be further. It's either there or there, depending -- I mean the scale of this -- with respect, Your Honours, the scale of this map, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could put a 4 against Pec.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's one of these two places here, so either here or here. This may be the pass into Montenegro beyond Pec itself. The third route, Your Honours, is down to this town here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll see if the lower half of the map from Pristina down can be brought up to a more visible scale.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive the map that you have presently marked with the markings you've identified, numbers 1 to 4 as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D382.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And now if we can have from the lower half, showing just Pristina and below. Is that easier for you to follow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, a little bit easier, yeah. We have Pristina up here, sir. Down towards through Lipljan and down to Stimlje, and the road was blocked in this area here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And if you could mark number 5 against that area. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was also the area of the Racak incident that was mentioned yesterday, Your Honour. And then the last route came down and then along the southern border here through the mountains of Strpci and into Prizren itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could mark Prizren with a number 6.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And it was this southern most one that was open through the period that I was being questioned about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you like this an exhibit now, Mr. Djurdjic? It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D383.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we please see this map one more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The one that is on the screen now or the earlier one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, a new map without markings. We have tendered this. No, the same area that you have shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please mark that one road that you mentioned from Pristina to Prizren?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll wait until we get an unmarked display. There it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Pristina and the southern -- the two southern routes, one went to Stimlje and was blocked just to the west of Stimlje. The alternative route was to go down further south and to turn off up into this area here, Strpci, and then on to Prizren as indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, but let me ask you, is it correct to say that from Pristina one had to go to Urosevac; and at Nerodimlje you had to deviate to Strpci; and over the Sar Planina, you had to go over the Sar Planina to get to Prizren. It was the so-called partisan route?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, from history, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that any different from what we saw on the previous map, Exhibit D383? The witness marked each of those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, could you please draw these two, three, lines for us to be able to get to Prizren. So Pristina, this lower line, and then Prizren, just draw a line so that we can see which rout had to be taken to Prizren.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, you come south from Prizren, pass Lipljan, on down to Urosevac. And then you turn west up into the Sar Planina, the mountain area, over and into Prizren which is here. This is the mountain area which Mr. Djurdjic is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And please draw the line up until Prizren. Finish it.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D384, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Defence Exhibit D005-0685.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, can you see in the heading, or the letterhead, this is a conversation that took place on the 25th of June between Mr. Milovan Negovanovic [as interpreted] and you. Do you know Mr. Milovan Negovanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, obviously I've not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us please turn to page 3 for the witness to be able to see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Negovan Jovanovic was the colonel who was in charge, Your Honours, of the foreign liaison service to which all defence attaches in Belgrade were accredited through to any interviews with people -- personnel in the Vojska Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, a little while ago we mentioned that and drew those maps, but here under item 2, Mr. Jovanovic is stating that the so-called KLA, that is, he is quoting your words. So I would like to know whether your position is reflected there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go back to that page where there is item 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Where it says the so-called KLA is increasingly revealing its fundamental characteristic of a terrorist organisation which has no qualms in liquidating its members for the slightest disobedience, something that has become more apparent recently. However, what is worrying is that the impression that the terrorists are controlling more and more territory. Of particular concern is the information that the following roads have been cut off and are under the control of the following communications: Kosovska-Mitrovica, Rudnik-Pec-Pristina-Komorane-Pec, and Timlje-Suva Reka-Prizren." Correction, Stimlje. Is that what you discussed with Mr. Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, sir, and as I've been attempting to imply to the Court that throughout the conflict from the beginning or middle of 1996 when I first went down to Kosovo until 1999, I saw my job as the defence attache to report accurately on both sides as the situation developed, and as is written here quite correctly and as I've indicated to the Court, that was the situation which was agreed to by Pukovnik Jovanovic and myself when we were speaking together on the date of this particular document. I think the point I would like to make is that having observed counter-insurgency operations in many areas, the terrorists are called by one man terrorists, by the other men freedom fighters. And it is up to the states in question as to how they deal with them. And what one was attempting to do was to provide correct information on the state of both sides in this particularly difficult conflict which I was privileged enough to observe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us please turn to page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, under item 3 it is stated that you pointed out as a particular problem the Yugoslav Albanian border and the prevention of future transfers of NVO, which is armaments and military equipment, and the infiltration of manpower from Albania.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And under 4 it is stated: "The main reason why the MZ," which stands for the international community, "failed to characterise the KLA as a terrorist organisation is the impact that the mass media and the reporting from KiM have, which is still in favour of the Albanians."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is I think a correct picture, sir. And If if you go down to the second paragraph, it says: "This is not the first time that Colonel Crosland has tried to convince us he is doing his utmost to have an objective view..." And I would maintain that that is exactly what my reports were. I reported on both sides as accurately as possible, fully respecting that within, then, the sovereign state of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the KLA was a freedom-fighter organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us go to page 3 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph, Colonel, it says: "He reiterated several times that his views were dismissed by the persons he talked to and the institution he informed, and that he had thus also, perhaps, jeopardized his career. He expressed his regrets at the official stances of the MZ, international community, and pointed out that it was his impression that the understanding of the KiM problem was slowly changing, which can be seen from the latest messages the MZ and NATO forwarded not only to the FRY authorities -- so forwarded not only to the FRY authorities, but also to the Albanians in KiM, regarding the cessation of the KLA's armed actions and the necessity to continue dialogue."

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've raised several points there, sir. My career -- it's a bit of a joke. I am a professional soldier, I speak as I see it. I'm not paid -- I'm paid to give proper, correct information. I made assessments as I saw it on the ground. I did learn Serbian, so I did understand your language to a reasonable degree. I, therefore, attempted to put the viewpoint from the Vojska Yugoslavia concerning what then, as I've stated before in court and under oath, the KLA was a terrorist organisation. I don't think I can be any more fairer than that. That having been said, as my reports have indicated on many occasions, unfortunately the disproportionate use of force throughout Kosova-Metohija resulted in very adverse publicity for the Serbian security forces. And as events have unfolded, Kosovo is now no longer part of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Sir, could you tell us at that time, that is in mid-1998 and in the summer of 1999, what kind of weapons did the KLA have?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, I've made many reports, and therefore the accuracy of those initial reports are what I would ask the Court to look at. If I remember correctly, in the early stages of this conflict, the KLA were fairly lightly armed with Kalashnikovs rifles, some rocket-propelled grenades. But as I've indicated, they were no match for the fire-power that could be brought to bear on them by the Serbian security forces. Later in 1998 and early 1999, there was a major improvement, as I've indicated in various reports, that the KLA had been resupplied with more up to date and more powerful, if you will, weaponry. But that is a summary. The detail would be in my reports, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information about artillery in the possession of the OVK with the range of 3 to 4 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that being mentioned, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And mortars of various calibres?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there may have been mortars at some stage, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Then RPG 7?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said to you earlier, sir, there were certainly -- I saw RPG and variants, I think in September or October, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statements you say that weapons were brought into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija via Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we again see map D002-4026. Can we see the southern portion of the map, please. Scroll up the Pristina part, so down from Pristina as much as possible. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you mark for us the route via which illegal weapons entered the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, Your Honours, this map is not easy to follow, but I'll try and mark some things. First of all, Prizren is here. This is the border between Albania and Kosovo. One of the routes was from Kukes down roughly in this area here, up through the mountainous area of Pastrik to the north-west of Prizren. Djakovica is here and again through this entire area across the mountains, there were many routes that would then be directed past Djakovica up towards Klina which is somewhere -- this map is very -- I think that's Suva Reka, up towards the Drenica which is roughly in this area up here, Your Honours. So this was the supply route and through this area here in Pec, to the west of Pec. Those in rough terms were some of the routes that we understood men and combat supplies were being brought in. And as I've mentioned in my statement to Pukovnik Jovanovic that this was an area of concern to the international community and to ourselves who were attempting to deal with the problem with the Serbian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Here you have underlined Malisevo. I should like to ask you in connection with your information about Malisevo in the beginning of summer in 1998.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, on what particular point do you want to question me on?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I should like to know whether the weapons which passed via the border was to be directed to Malisevo and then to Drenica, and, in fact, whether the KLA headquarters was in Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, sir, that was one of the major headquarters I visited. Several of these headquarters in Drenica, Vojcnak [phoen], Lausa, Mitrovica, Bajgora, and south of Pristina in the area of Magora [phoen]. So I visited several of the headquarters. And as to your specific question of whether the weapons went through Malisevo, I couldn't possibly tell you. But one would presume that in any organisation there was a direction, and we understood the direction was towards the area of Drenica, just to the west of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I seek to tender this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D385, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we see Exhibit 927 which is on the 65 ter list. Could we turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, these minutes from a meeting of the collegium of the General Staff of the 29th of June, 1998. And in it Major-General Branislav Milovanovic, as you can see at the very beginning, underlines the measures that NATO is planning to put in place or has already executed, a part of which in the context of the resolution of the Kosovo crisis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Here he gives some NATO data, and on page 3, rather page 2, I'm sorry: "The strength of the KLA is about 3.000 men. It's best trained section numbers about 500 people, divided into groups of five to six? They are mostly equipped with light infantry arms and mortars -- and throwers. And Most of them brought from Albania. According to available information, their combat training is organised in camps in Albanian territory, more specifically in Bajram Curi, Kukes. It is conducted by Albanians, former JNA officers, Mujahedin, and Muslims from Bosnia. Since the end of 1998, the Kosovo Liberation Army leadership has been taking measures to strengthen the combat power of its units. For the purpose of protecting settlements, the structure of the armed formations has been re-organised on the clan principle." Is this the information that was available to NATO at this particular time, namely in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to that question. That is outside the scope of knowledge of this witness. I don't know why he is being asked about information available to NATO at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: First, is this document one dated in 1998? I thought it was a 1999 document. It's reporting in the paragraph from which you've just been reading, "since the end of 1998 the KLA leadership has been taking measures," which suggests that it is a 1999 document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to read it the way it is written, but obviously it is a mistake. The date is the 29th of June, 1998, and General Milovanovic is adducing data that are available to NATO, that are in the possession of NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You are suggesting that the document is correctly identified on the first page as a June 1998 document, and that there is an error in the date end of 1998 in the last paragraph on the page that's now open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not only that, Your Honours, but also in the translation into English. It is mistakenly misstated 29th of June, 1999. That is also a mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We seem to be doing very well with mistakes. Whatever the date then, which is a matter of uncertainty, whether it is June 1998 or 1999, the question perhaps for Mr. Crosland is whether he is in a position to verify what is reported as the knowledge of NATO about forces. Can you help us with that, Mr. Crosland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'll try. In any counter-insurgency operation the ability to accurately state what a terrorist organisation has, its strengths, what we would call its order of battle, I would suggest is usually exaggerated for very obvious reasons, because the security forces would rather be facing slightly less than what they put on paper for the reasons of securing the force with which to deal with the problem. The figures that are mentioned here of -- are hard core of, whatever it is, 3-, 4-, 500, and about 3.000 in total, I wouldn't disagree with. As I've said, it's always very difficult to tie down counter-terrorist forces because obviously they are very covert and wary of their security and don't really wish to advertise that they are larger or smaller than is anticipated or is reported in the news. I don't know whether if that helps Your Honours or not. But these figures I would -- I wouldn't disagree with them in principle. And the two areas mentioned, Bajram Curi and Kukes were forward operating bases, if that's the correct term, in Albania from where considerable reinforcement of the KLA took place throughout 1998 and 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Are you able to comment on whether these numbers or something like them would be known at that time to NATO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I suspect within the NATO intelligence hierarchy they had good access to what was close to these numbers, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that help you, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does, but the colonel is modest here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What is your contribution to the information that was available to NATO?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as you are well aware, I am but one small pebble on the beach. I, as I've indicated to you, reported as factually and as accurately as possible, and my assessment from Kosova-Metohija would be placed alongside other intelligence sources, and these would all be mixed together to come out with a possibly more accurate, possibly not so accurate, picture of what was happening on the ground in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of your constant contacts as the defence attache with the foreign liaison section of the VJ and of the Ministry of Defence, do you know that in July 1999 [as interpreted], the chief of the General Staff requested from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that measures be taken against the Republic of Albania in view of the assistance they were rendering to the KLA, logistical assistance in materiels in terms of expertise, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I recall that I was shown by either Colonel Negovan Jovanovic, or General Dimitrijevic a map on which the Vojska Yugoslavia had portrayed the incidents on the border that they said had happened. I have no reason to particularly -- I looked at the board, and the number of incidents seem, to me, reasonably true. I was grateful for that information which I relayed back to my Ministry of Defence, as I said, by way of indicating the seriousness of the situation and what might happen in the future. So that was valuable intelligence from our point of view, and I forwarded it back to my superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 25, line 2, it is stated in July 1999, whereas it should be July 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It appears to be another of those unresolved questions, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would not have intervened, but the infallible Marie O'Leary warned me of this fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Did the Army of Yugoslavia, the VJ, present data that in the first half of 1998 from -- seven soldiers [realtime transcript read in error "747"] had been killed by KLA fire and that over 40 had been wounded?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me if I remember that specific detail, I'm afraid I can't recall. I was, as I indicated to you just now, I was shown a map of the incidents that had happened mainly along the border because that was the primacy of the Vojska Yugoslavia at that particular phase of the campaign. As to this -- the particular incident that you speak about, I can't, in all honesty, recall that. If I have mentioned it somewhere in one of my reports, I apologise, but I can't recall it, truthfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, at page 25, line 24, you are quoted as having suggested, "747 members of the VJ killed by KLA fire." I think your suggestion was much more modest, was it not? Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I said seven wounded and -- seven killed and 40 wounded. And the interpreters remark it was interpreted as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we talked a lot about the village of Prilep. Am I right when I say that in that area there was permanent fighting from 1998 until up to the point when you -- or throughout your stay in the FRY until March 1999?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I mentioned yesterday to the Court, the road going north from Djakovica to Decani and on to Pec was in all aspects the front line. And yes, the area around Prilep, which was a -- by the roadside there, there was a small MUP position that was probably continuously under fire, or on a daily basis under fire, I should say, from the KLA in that area. I wouldn't -- I've reported that on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that the KLA also opened fire at Prilep from a distance?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct, sir, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you then agree with me when I say that the area of fighting between the KLA and the forces of the FRY actually resulted in the damage to the facilities in between, because both sides were interested in the road, in the communication which passes through that particular village?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inevitably damage was occurred between the two forces with fighting. I refer you back to my reports where, again, there were pictures taken of Prilep, and I have no idea where they are now, but Prilep was literally 20 centimetres high. All the houses had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, Colonel, have you seen the photographs that you referred to just now during the proceedings, during the trial?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason I'm thinking, Your Honours, is again I've made many visits to the court. I can't remember that these photographs were sent back to the Ministry of Defence and whether these were handed over along with most of my reports, I'm not privilege to know that action.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave aside the other cases, the other trials for now, but at this trial you have not seen those photographs?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on this particular time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that you are taking a sip of your water, and I believe, Your Honours, it is time for our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it's a convenient time, is it, Mr. Djurdjic? We will have the first break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I would like to dwell on Prilep for awhile. Do you remember that in November MUP members were killed there and that their vehicle was hit by an anti-armour projectile? Have you heard my question, sir? Do you remember that in November 1998 a vehicle was hit by an anti-armour weapon which resulted in the deaths of some MUP members in the village of Prilep?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't specifically recall this incident where three members of the security forces were killed. However, as I said in the earlier session, that it was clear there had been a resupply of more powerful weapons to the KLA in October/November, and yes, I saw in one of the headquarters anti-personnel or anti -- sorry, rocket-propelled grenades. This was -- as I indicated earlier to the Court, this road from Djakovica to Celani [phoen] Pec was the front line for many months from March up until the finish of the campaign, so there were many such incidents along this stretch of road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document D005-0043. Page 1978 toward the end, and then 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's question says: "On the 20th of November, two Serbian police officers both from the north-east of Serbia were killed and four were wounded at Prilep near Decani where their vehicle was hit by an anti-armour weapon." And on page 1979, lines 22 and 23 says: "Their vehicle was hit by an anti-armour weapon, what does that mean?" And you are quoted as saying at the bottom of the page: "Very close to this time, I can't exactly remember the date, but I visited the KLA headquarters here at Riznik, close by Riznik, which is the zone of Ramush Haradinaj, and they were very keen to show us off a new range of automatic weapons; sniper rifles; and Panzerfaust, which were anti-tank weapons; sniper rifles which had just arrived on the latest resupply from Albania, through the old corridor I mentioned," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And -- but the KLA, when they missed their target and hit a building, do they not demolish buildings with such weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there will be damage, sir, yes. One accepts that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask you something else, something I should have asked you at the beginning, but I didn't remember. Did you know that the political objective of the KLA was the cessation of Kosovo and Metohija from the Republic of Serbia by means of armed force, that is -- in other words, by force, and the creation of a greater Albania?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I took up my position as defence attache in Belgrade in July 1996, I studied as best as I could the very complex history of this whole area in the Balkans, and the various conflicts that had taken place going back to Kosovo Polje in 1389, and the claims of Albanians to Velika Albania, greater Albania. I can't say I completely understood the problem, I'm not certain many people did. It's very complex. So within history, there was always this claim that Velika Albania, greater Albania, might include Kosovo, might also include Macedonia. And depending on which set of historical maps you look at, you can see this problem displayed in many ways. So one presumes that this was part of the KLA's, Kosovo Liberation Army's aims, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the first part which matters more to me, that Kosovo and Metohija should secede from Serbia by use of force?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I think I can remember that being a stated aim of the KLA when discussions were carried out with the KLA. When I met them, one reminded them that Kosovo was a part of the sovereign state, former Yugoslavia, and therefore they had a fairly major problem to achieve this particular aim. And this had been stated by President Milosevic very forcibly in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, sir, the declaration of the KLA, dated 29 April 1998? It was published in the Bujku paper.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't come readily to mind, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see Exhibit D005-0443, page 1905.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you can see your reply to the Prosecutor's question: We can pass over to the report dated 14 April, and I'm interested in paragraphs 3 and 4. Sorry, 30th of April. "The KLA issued a nine-point statement on the 29th of April, published in Bujku, the mass circulation radically inclined Albanian language Pristina newspaper, saying that the homeland was in a state of war and was fighting to liberate and unify Albania's occupied territories. The statement called on Albanians," as said, "to review their stand. It was a duty of the free part of their homeland to help the occupied part. The KLA was ready to strike against the enemy at the right time. However, the KLA was ready to take part in talks with the enemy, but only after the occupying troops had left and with the mediation of a third party. Any agreement without its presence would be invalid. The statement appealed to the frustrated and faint-hearted who were trying to plunge the people into defeatism and anarchy and who were trying to remove themselves from the scene." Do you remember that telegram you sent on the 30th of April 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the greatest of respect, sir, as I've said many times, I can't remember every single report. If that is what was sent then, then that is the statement that I would stand by. And I think, as I've explained to the Court just now, that these statements were coming out all the time from the Kosovo Liberation Army, and one was attempting to report the progress or lack of it on both sides as various incidents happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In line 16 through 19, the question was: "Mr. Crosland, just specifically referring to the statement that the homeland was in a state of war and was fighting to liberate and unify Albanian occupied territories, did you ever while you were there at the time come across those kinds of statements from KLA members?" And you answered in lines 20 through 23, on page 1905: "Yes, Your Honours. All the time was the view put forward by the KLA and other personnel, that this was a mission to retake what was called by the Serbs Velika Albania, greater Albania..." et cetera. These are your words from the Limaj case.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I don't have any problem with that. That is a statement which I stand by, and I think I've tried to explain to the Court it was the situation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, do you remember what the situation in the field was like in mid-July 1998?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've said many times to the Court, the situation was very fluid with one side getting the upper-hand and then the other side retaliating all through the area of the period of 1998 until the security forces, as I've said again in many reports, seemed to begin a more concentrated effort to clear the major routes across Kosovo in September/October of 1998. But during that entire period, as I've tried to make it clear, attacks from the KLA and retaliation from the Serb security forces were a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In this trial I see that your reports from early June until the 7th of August, I believe, are missing. So there is a gap. And I think you said that you were at Malisevo on the 1st of July, 1998, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It will be in one of my reports, yes. I think that was the first time we went into Malisevo, yes. If I remember correctly. I apologise if it's wrong. The reason there may be a gap is because our eldest daughter got married in England and notwithstanding the situation in the Balkans I was ordered home by the boss, my wife, to attend the wedding.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, your wife is right, but we have a report that you returned on the 25th of June, which means that from that date on you were present here. But you went there, if I'm not mistaken, to verify whether at Malisevo there was the OVK -- sorry, the KLA headquarters at that time.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what did you find out, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that date is correct, and I accept that that may be the date, and forgive me if it's wrong, we drove north from Orahovac out of Serb control into a KLA check-point. We were stopped and searched. We were then escorted into Malisevo, and my report of that particular occurrence mentions the facts, some of which I can recall. Along the road there were very minor defensive positions, small trenches, on the way to Malisevo. In Malisevo I seem to recall there were probably, I don't know, 100, 150 KLA. Some were dressed in black which appeared to be their police equivalent. And I was interviewed for, I think, three hours. We were then -- I said if I was not released there would be problems because I was expected in Djakovica to meet other people, and eventually the KLA decided to release me and my warrant officer to continue our journey northwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Page 1952 corroborates that you are right. On pages 24 and 25 you were asked why you had gone to Malisevo on the 1st of July. You gave the same answer that you have just repeated. Is it correct that you were first stopped by a man who looked oriental to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one particularly unpleasant individual who, yes, was of Middle East appearance. I think there were also, and I think in my report it states that there may well have been fighters from other countries from Europe attracted to the area, as we all know, during all the Balkan conflicts. There have been mercenaries who have come to engage in a cause, which gives them a job to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you speak to that individual, and if so, in what language did you speak with that soldier who was unpleasant?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, sir, he would not engage in any form of conversation, and if I remember correctly, he was the only person who was openly hostile towards myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked this question because I know that you were in the Middle East so you may have been able to communicate with that person in Arabic, but it appears that you didn't. Who was the chief of that staff at Malisevo? Did you identify the person amongst those fighters?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, it might well be in my report. You are asking me now under oath. I can't, to be honest, remember the names of various individuals, so I don't wish to make a statement which is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Anybody can make a mistake especially after so much time, but if the Main Staff is at Malisevo, and you went there to establish whether that was the case, then probably after initial difficulties you wanted to meet someone who was in charge, a commander of that staff, and were you able to reach the commander on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think with respect, sir, you are slightly simplifying the situation. My warrant officer and myself were -- we carried the licna karta, the identity card of Yugoslavia, which was not recognised by the KLA. They had, in effect, captured us in their terms. And I was taken at gun point to the headquarters, which I've identified before was in a black and white building in the centre of Malisevo, and I was interviewed, it was more interrogation if one is quite blunt, and I was more concerned with the welfare of my warrant officer who was on his own outside. And, therefore, this discussion, if we are going to put it correctly, took place between me and a number of members of the KLA whose names at this, 12 years on, I cannot remember. But the situation was not as peaceful as you suggest. There was a fair degree of hostility towards us which is understandable if you are dealing with counter-insurgency forces. They are obviously concerned about their own security and the fact that you may be threatening that security by visiting their location. So one understands that and you behave in a fairly guarded manner, or both sides behave in a guarded manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but you stood up to the challenge and went there. And thank God you were released, many weren't. But you went to Malisevo again on the 25th of July, what was it that prompted you to do that on the 25th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the defence attache accredited to the former Yugoslavia and the VJ, I was entitled under my accreditation to travel anywhere within former Yugoslavia apart from areas specifically given to me as being out of bounds. I did not recognise the authority of the KLA and, therefore, insisted that I was totally within my rights to travel on this particular road. Now, I knew the risks concerned, but in order to try and, as I said, report as accurately and as fairly as possible on both sides of the problem, I decided to carry out this particular visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I haven't interrupted you so far and I don't wish to do so in the future, but for the sake of time economy, I would ask you to give shorter answers. But when you went to Malisevo on the 1st of July to see whether there was a headquarters there, why did you go there again on the 25th of July? That was my question. Had you -- whether or not you had established contacts with the KLA in the meantime, it's better for you to explain than for me to elaborate.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I can only repeat. And Your Honour, a question of time for the sake, I won't repeat it. I went to Malisevo on the second visit in order to see if there were any changes to the first visit. And that's part of a principle of gaining intelligence. You can go and see an incident on one occasion, and then when you return to that particular incident or place, the situation can have changed. And that is why, as I did around the whole area in the Drenica and around western Kosovo and so on and so forth, I would go back on repeated times to see what the situation was, how it had developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And had anything changed on the 25th of July when you were there? And who received you at the KLA headquarters? And what was the conversation about?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, if you are asking specific details, and without wishing to report erroneously to the Court, I must refer you back to the reports that I wrote at the time. And if you produce those reports, then the Court can see the detail of my reports as and when I wrote them. To ask me to repeat things some like 12 years later on I think is -- does not do anyone's understanding of the situation -- doesn't make it any better, or clearer, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Colonel, can I ask you this: In the area from Orahovac to Malisevo, had the situation changed in any way between the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, I did not hear the other date. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall repeat the question; it wasn't heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, according to your information, had anything happened and had the situation changed between the 17th of July and the 25th of July 1998 in the area between Orahovac and Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with respect, my reports of those dates, if they are correct, I'm sure they are, will be what is written in those reports is the most accurate version I can give. And, therefore, I can't recall the specific reports to hand. As I said, I would ask to you look at those reports and then we can discuss them, if that is what is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you recall that on the 17th of July Orahovac fell into the hands of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to recall that that was correct. Orahovac was a very important area, not least of all because it supplied an awful lot of [indiscernible] to the whole of Serbia. So There were a lot of businesses in Orahovac that really didn't want anything to do with either side of the military organisations. They wanted to get on with their business of making wine and continue their lives without being interrupted. So if that is the date the city was retaken, then I would accept it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: By the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And from the 17th to the 25th, do you also remember other places that were taken by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, with respect, I've said many times, the situation flowed backwards and forwards. As one side moved forward, the other side moved back. And, therefore, the reports that I made at the time would indicate the ebb and the flow of that particular conflict. But as to specific dates 12 years from the time it happened, I can only refer you back to my reports at the time, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statements and your reports you say that the forces of the FRY on the 25th when you were leaving, i.e., when you left Malisevo, actually launched an action to liberate Malisevo. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in my report, sir, yes, and that is correct. There were two, as I've stated, two combat teams on the Lapusnik and Kijevo on the main Pristina-Pec road, and we came across these two combat groups that were preparing to carry out an assault on to Malisevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember returning again and, I don't think that I am mistaken, with the defence attache of the United States in September -- in August to Malisevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is in a report, sir, then that report is correct. That was the one written at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have on the screen Defence Exhibit D005-0697. That is a video.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going object to this video on the same grounds that I objected to the earlier video. We have no information as to the providence of this video. We don't know who filmed it, where it was filmed, when it was filmed, so we are unable to know anything about the locality that's shown on the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Once again we'll see whether the witness is able to assist. If not, well, then it can't be an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you recognise the place that we just saw in this video footage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir. That is the area of Malisevo. There is a report of mine that shows the incident of the armoured personnel carrier being hit by a mine, and that is in one of my reports. The interview being carried out by the MUP pukovnik was shown on Dnevnik on the local television. I think, if I may suggest, the point you are trying to make is the village is without damage. I would say that, yes, this happened before the incident we are talking about when the Serb forces decided to go in and clear the area of Malisevo. I would humbly remind yourself that I took around members of the Trojka and the G8, many ambassadors, including Lord Ashdown on two occasions, and they themselves saw massive wanton damage. But at this particular stage, Malisevo was untouched, but it did not remain so, because the shops where the jewellery and the costume, which I can actually remember since you've shown me the picture, that whole area was subsequently destroyed. And a further village just outside of Malisevo where there was a school, I picked up 12, 120-millimetre shells that had been fired into the school itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. This is the 29th of July news reel, 1998 of course. And it is true that you were there also subsequently. You left it on the 25th, and according to your statement, you returned to Malisevo on the 29th to see what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to seek to tender this exhibit, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will become Exhibit D386, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher for us to again see the video D005-0698.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And once again, Your Honour, I object to the use of this video on the same grounds as the earlier video that was shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise this footage, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears to be footage of Malisevo, but, my comments are exactly the same. When that was taken, I don't know. If you are questioning the accuracy of my reports, then all I can offer to the Court is that you have to go back to view the original reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this exhibit also. This is the 16th of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I obtained this footage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The video will be received, but it needs to be made clear, Mr. Djurdjic, that we have no evidence as to the date of the recording of any of these videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, this is a slip-up on my part because I did not bring the material from which it is evident what I ask for and what I received from the archives of the RTS. But this exhibit was used in the Milutinovic case. But I shall do so subsequently, rest assured.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The video will become Exhibit D387, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Defence document D176.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a directive of the General Staff of the VJ of the 28th of July, 1998. GROM-1998. And you are familiar with this document, you've seen it before. In this first passage under 1, Roman numeral I, the Chief of Staff is providing data on the number of members of the insurgence, as you refer to them.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect, sir, that is the estimate of the General Staff of the VJ. And as I've said, that's their take, their estimate of the problem that they are facing. And the numbers, as I've already indicated to the Court, could be less or could be larger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. In the context that you had with General Perisic, did he reiterate these data that you can see in this directive to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, sir, you are asking me very specific questions and very specific dates that were -- or may have been referred to in my reports at that period. Therefore, to comment in general terms under oath is not something I'm prepared to do. If I made a statement, then could I humbly suggest that it's presented, and we can discuss that statement. But you are asking me to make an assertion on events, as I said, 12 years ago where there are or there may be relevant reports which are critical to this part of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I told you that I wish to ask you questions that you haven't been asked by others, and I ask you this question because the meeting with the Chief of General Staff at the time in which this directive was adopted or thereafter was, after all, an event that one should recall and would recall. And I know that you have not seen this directive, but I ask you whether through contacts and conversations - and you did say that you had conversations with General Perisic - he ever referred to the kind of numbers that we saw here? This is the kind of forces that he referred to. So do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: With great respect, in very general terms I've already said, yes. But if you are going to be more specific about it, then we need to get back into the dirt and find these particular reports. But in general terms, these were the figures that the Vojska Yugoslavia briefed people on and that is their appreciation of the situation at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now scroll down to Roman numeral III. It ought to be on page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this chapter is about the engagement of the Yugoslav Army, and we have the first stage which is: "In the zone of the Pristina Corps, secure the state border towards the republic of Albania and Macedonia, with both increased intensity and in depth, while in the zone of the 2nd army and navy, with increased intensity. In the zone of the Pristina Corps, protect the units and military facilities from the operations of the sabotage and terrorist forces and secure that the Yugoslav Army units supply routes are passable. By quick action in conjunction with the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, overwhelm and destroy the sabotage and terrorist forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija according to a special order from the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army." My question is, were you familiar or acquainted with such a role in engagement of the army in the period after the adoption of this directive in context with members of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, if I remember correctly, sir, it was not until General Ojdanic addressed the Belgrade Attache Association, I think it was the 27th of August, where it was made clear for the first time that the Vojska Yugoslavia was engaged in counter-terrorist operations in Kosovo and Metohija. As I've stated many times, the Vojska Yugoslavia aims in Kosovo were to secure the international border between Albania and Macedonia and Kosovo to a distance of, I think, 2, perhaps 5 kilometres, to secure the Pristina Corps bases, their exercise areas, and also to secure the lines of communication throughout Kosovo, which as I've stated many times, was then a sovereign part of former Yugoslavia. I have no problems with any of these particular aims, as I've said to you on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come back to what you have just said, but for the sake of continuity, can we see D177 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now here we have an order by the commander of the 3rd Army of the 29th of July, 1998. Do you agree that this is an order which is based on the directives that we saw just awhile ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the normal command process in that the chief of the General Staff gives his orders to his field commander. In this case, the commander Nis [as interpreted], and then he would give his orders down to the operational commander of the Pristina Corps within the operational area of Kosovo. And, I think, if I may just add, that this is -- just backs up what I said sometime ago, that the Serbian security forces were winding themselves up for a major operation after August time, which is what I've said on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should now like to show you a document, the number of which is D167.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, these are the rules of service of the Yugoslav Army which were in force in the relevant period that we are now discussing. I should like to ask you to take a look at Article 473. Is it fair to say, Colonel, that according to this article of the rules of service, units of the army may be used to counter outlawed sabotage terrorists and other armed enemy groups, or to prevent or eliminate a state of emergency under a decision by the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Supreme Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I wouldn't beg to differ on this at all. All I would offer to the Court is that there is proportionate force and disproportionate force. How a nation deals with a counter-insurgency operation, as we are currently seeing in some of the troubled areas of the world today, is a matter for the national bodies that control those particular countries. In this particular case, I think without any doubt, there is clear evidence that there was massive destruction and movement of personnel who, on the whole, were not initially engaged against the Serbian security forces. I was in the position of having to report this process which I have attempted to do with very detailed reports which cover this entire area. The order from the Chief of the General Staff is an order that that gentleman must defend, and I'm not going to comment on a senior general's orders to his troops who are going to carry out his orders.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CROSLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I call document D004-3006. Can we see it on the screen, please. Sorry, I was just corrected. It is Exhibit D331.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this is a report of the forward command post of the 3rd Army sent to the General Staff on the 9th of August, 1998. Let us skip Roman numeral I and continue with Roman numeral II, the first paragraph. Am I right when I say that the commander of the 3rd Army reports to the Chief of General Staff about the activities?
